transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-09-24 14:30 UTC | Duration: 75 mins
Attendees: Jamie Patel (Redwood AE); Lina Zhao (Redwood SE); Marcus Lee (Orion - Head of Platform); Priya Natarajan (Orion SRE); Evan Ross (Orion Data Eng); Sana Ahmed (Orion Security)
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20250924-orion-001 (note: link placeholder)

Summary:
- Deep dive on integrating OpenTelemetry (OTel/OTLP) for token-level metrics and traces from Redwood runtime in Orion's VPC/on-prem environment.
- Discussed tradeoffs: trace sampling vs token-level metrics retention, cardinality concerns, cost, and privacy.
- Action items: share OTel collector config for VPC sidecar, Orion to export sample traces, schedule pilot for batching/quantization benchmarks.

Topics covered:
- OTLP endpoint placement (sidecar vs central collector) in VPCs
- Token-level span attributes and histogram metrics (token_latency_ms, token_size, kv_cache_hit)
- Correlating traces with Redwood Console request_ids and logs
- Batching, continuous batching effects on tail latency, and KV cache observability
- Quantization mode metrics: int8 vs fp16 comparisons
- High-cardinality tags and retention strategies

Transcript:
00:00:00 Jamie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We thought we'd do a focused runtime->observability deep dive — Lina will lead on the OTel specifics and I'll handle next steps and pricing. Marcus, you said you wanted token-level fidelity and trace linking into your existing stack?
00:00:22 Marcus (Orion): Yeah sorry for the late join, quick yes. We need per-token latency and cache hit signals so we can tune batching and also detect regressions when model updates roll.
00:00:37 Lina (Redwood SE): Great. Quick high-level: Redwood can emit both metrics and traces. For heavy production use we recommend sending dense metrics (Prom-compatible histograms) for token latency distributions and sparse traces for sampled requests. That keeps storage sane.
00:00:54 Priya (Orion SRE): When you say "emit" — are we talking a sidecar collector in our VPC, or will Redwood push to a public OTLP endpoint? Network policy and data controls are big for us.
00:01:12 Lina: Good question. We support two patterns: 1) Sidecar/daemonset in your cluster that exports OTLP to your internal collector (preferred for on-prem/VPC), or 2) a secure OTLP endpoint that you expose to Redwood (mutual TLS + client cert). For on-prem we usually recommend the sidecar so zero egress is necessary.
00:01:34 Sana (Security): And certificates/KMS? We need keys in our HSM.
00:01:40 Lina: You can terminate TLS at your collector, and we support client mTLS. For any credential management we integrate with your KMS — we have config examples in the otel-collector-vpc.yaml I'll share.
00:02:02 Evan (Orion): I want to understand the actual signal set. What attributes do you put on spans and what metrics do you recommend?
00:02:12 Lina: Good — here's an example: every request gets a top-level span with attributes: request_id, model (e.g., redwood-inc/rwkv-v2), deployment_id, customer_id (low-cardinality), sequence_length, batch_size, quant_mode. Inside the request we optionally emit token spans — each token span has token_index, token_latency_ms, kv_cache_hit(true|false), cache_response_ms.
00:02:44 Marcus: Token spans sound high-cardinality and heavy. Won't that blow up our traces and cost?
00:02:51 Lina: Exactly, so we usually do token spans at a sample rate — e.g., 1% of requests or use an adaptive sampler that increases sampling on anomalies. For full coverage we recommend metrics: a histogram metric token_latency_ms bucketed per model+quant_mode+bucketed_seq_len and a count metric kv_cache_hits_total with labels for hit/miss. That gives you the distribution without token-by-token trace volume.
00:03:20 Priya: How do we correlate a metric spike with a specific trace to debug?
00:03:25 Lina: We include request_id as a span attribute and as a metric label for a small set of high-cardinality debugging exports. Then when your metrics alert triggers you can increase sampling for that window and capture full token spans for a subset of requests.
00:03:40 Evan: Do you emit histograms as Prom histograms? We use Prometheus + Grafana internally.
00:03:46 Lina: Yes — the collector converts OTLP metrics into Prom histograms for ingestion. We also provide example dashboards for Grafana that map token latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), per-model throughput, and cache hit heatmaps. We'll share the JSON dashboards.
00:04:03 Marcus: One more thing — our apps are multi-tenant. We can't have raw prompt text in telemetry.
00:04:10 Lina: We redact prompt content by default from spans — we only emit token-level latency and token_index. If you need token-level debug you can enable redaction exceptions in a secure environment and route those traces to a restricted retention bucket.
00:04:27 Sana: Retention TTLs — what do you suggest?
00:04:30 Lina: Typical is 30d for detailed token metrics if you want to keep historical latency trends; 90d for aggregated histograms. Traces usually 7-30d depending on compliance. We can align with your data retention policies.
00:04:45 Marcus: Can we surface KV cache hit ratios in a dashboard? We want to know how much prefix reuse is saving us.
00:04:52 Lina: Absolutely — kv_cache_hit_ratio = kv_cache_hits_total / kv_cache_requests_total. We also emit a per-prefix cache age metric so you can see staleness.
00:05:05 Evan: On quantization — when we flip to int8 we expect more throughput but sometimes higher latency variance. Can you quantify that?
00:05:12 Lina: In our runtime we tag the execution path with quant_mode and emit CPU/GPU utilization, ops/sec, and token_latency_ms per quant_mode. In our internal benchmarks int8 increased tokens/sec by ~1.8-2.4x on T4-ish hardware but p99 tail latency can widen for certain prompt shapes. We'll run that in your environment during the pilot.
00:05:38 Priya: The batching piece — we're sensitive to tail latency. How do continuous batching and dynamic batching play with the token metrics?
00:05:46 Lina: Continuous batching aggregates incoming tokens into micro-batches with a short window to maximize throughput. That reduces cost but can increase p95/p99. We emit batch_size_distribution and batch_wait_ms metrics. With token-level histograms you can see per-batch latency contributions. We can also trace KV cache hits across batch boundaries by linking spans using the request_id and sub-span for cache lookups.
00:06:12 Marcus: If we route traces to Datadog or Splunk, any gotchas?
00:06:18 Lina: Nothing major but note that high-cardinality labels (like request_id) are expensive in many SaaS tracing backends. For SaaS integrations we recommend sampling and limiting exported labels — keep request_id for sampled traces only. For metrics, reduce cardinality by using buckets (seq_len_small/medium/large) rather than raw lengths.
00:06:38 Evan: How real-time are the metrics? We want near real-time dashboards for incident response.
00:06:43 Lina: With typical OTLP->Prometheus pipelines you'll get 5-10s scrape intervals in a well-tuned setup, but if you need sub-second token telemetry that's more of an event stream to an analytics pipeline. For most SRE use cases, 5-15s is adequate.
00:07:00 Priya: Any recommended alerts?
00:07:03 Lina: Baseline p95 token latency by model+quant_mode; alert on >30% deviation. Cache hit ratio drop >10% over 1h. Sudden increase in batch_wait_ms or batch_size variance. We'll give rule examples.
00:07:18 Marcus: Ok great. Can you show a quick mockup of a dashboard we can use?
00:07:22 Lina: Sure — I have a shared Grafana JSON and a Redwood Console screenshot. (note: Lina screenshares)
00:07:40 [screen description omitted in transcript]
00:07:55 Evan: There's a question about on-prem collectors — we run a private k8s cluster with restricted egress. Will your sidecar require outbound connection to Redwood?
00:08:03 Lina: No — sidecar -> your local collector -> your storage. Redwood does not require outbound egress for metrics if you host your collector. If you want Redwood to receive traces for managed debugging we can establish a peered secure connection or you can push a periodic sanitized bundle.
00:08:25 Marcus: Ok that fits our security model. What about resource overhead — CPU/GPU cost for emitting these spans and metrics?
00:08:33 Lina: Metrics emission is lightweight. Token spans will have some overhead when enabled at high sample rates. We measured about 2-5% CPU overhead for 1% token-span sampling and <1% for basic metrics and histograms.
00:08:50 Priya: For pilot, how do we run a comparison of batching/quantization?
00:08:56 Lina: We'll run side-by-side runs: fixed load replay of your sample traffic with three configs (fp16 baseline, int8 quantized, int8 with different KV cache policy) and collect token_latency_ms histograms, batch_wait_ms, throughput, and cache_hit_ratio. We'll provide a spreadsheet with results and plots.
00:09:20 Jamie (Redwood AE): I'll also include dedicated capacity pricing for the pilot and a quick SOW template.
00:09:28 Marcus: One last thing — regulatory: we need an audit log of who accessed traces and when.
00:09:34 Lina: Redwood Console supports audit logs and RBAC; we can show role-based access and retention controls. We'll include a sample audit log export.
00:09:46 Sana: We'll need SOC2 artifacts before pilot starts.
00:09:50 Jamie: Noted — I'll attach our SOC2+ISO docs in the follow-up email.
00:10:00 [discussion of calendar scheduling and timezones, quick coordination noise omitted]
00:12:40 Wrap / recap:
- Lina to share otel-collector-vpc.yaml, Grafana dashboard JSON, and example Redwood Console dashboard mock.
- Orion to export 48h of token-level metrics and sample traces (anonymized).
- Plan: 1-week pilot, run replayed traffic, compare quantization profiles.

Closing:
Jamie: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the configs and a proposed pilot plan.
Marcus: Thanks, appreciate the level of detail. We'll get the sample traces to you.
